extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, literary critics, and students of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and critical guidance for writing and judging novels: definitions, core aspects (Story; People; Plot; Fantasy; Prophecy; Pattern and Rhythm), and techniques for character, narrative, and form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel definition (length and form)
rubrics_metrics.description: “A fiction in prose of a certain extent.” Forster adds a practical proviso: any fictitious prose work over 50,000 words will be a novel for the purposes of these lectures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (to include or consider): The Pilgrim’s Progress, Ulysses, Rasselas, etc., are discussed to test the boundary; the 50,000-word floor is a pragmatic rule-of-thumb rather than metaphysical definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Story (fundamental aspect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental aspect of the novel is its story-telling aspect: the story is a narrative of events arranged in their time sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary merit of a story is to make the audience want to know what happens next (suspense as the backbone—Scheherazade example). Forster calls the story backbone (or tapeworm) and warns that while essential, story alone is a low form of literary achievement; other aspects must be balanced against pure plotting-for-suspense.

rubrics_metrics.name: People (characterization: round vs flat)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes two main types of characters: 'flat' characters (constructed around a single idea or quality) and 'round' characters (complex, capable of surprising the reader yet remaining consistent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flat characters are serviceable, memorable, often comic or emblematic; round characters carry the novel’s human truth and can change or reveal new facets. Forster emphasizes reading characters closely, looking for the 'novelist’s touch', and avoiding crude stereotyping.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Plot (pattern, unity vs life’s richness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot provides a unifying pattern (hour-glass, converging lines, cathedral-like unity) that organizes events, but a rigid external pattern can shut out the richness of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: over-rigid patterns that force life to conform to art (resulting in exercises rather than living fiction). Pro-pattern guidance: seek unity but not at the expense of life; prefer flexible forms or internal stitching (rhythm, motifs) to oppressive external designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern (external shape) — advantages and dangers
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern (an imposed external unity or shape) can create beauty but tends to exclude the messy richness of human life and can leave the reader feeling 'beautifully done, but not worth doing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept pattern when it arises naturally from subject/plot; beware of pattern-for-its-own-sake. In drama pattern may be more acceptable than in the novel because the novel must admit human bulk and variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm (internal repetition plus variation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhythm in fiction is defined as repetition plus variation; it acts as internal stitching that can hold a large, ill-constructed work together and produce beauty without rigid external form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use motifs (the Proustian 'little phrase' example) that recur, vary, and develop across the book to create internal unity. Bad rhythm hardens into symbol and bores (e.g., mechanical repeating banners); good rhythm waxes and wanes to give surprise and freshness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of rhythm (local motif vs large-scale symphonic effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Easy rhythm: local, tappable repetitions (motifs, phrases). Difficult rhythm: an overarching relation between large blocks (analogous to a symphony’s total shape).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Easy rhythm can be achieved in many novels (motifs, recurring imagery); the analogous large-scale symphonic unity in fiction is rarer and harder to demonstrate, though some works (e.g., War and Peace) approach an expansive, chord-like effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final test: affection (reader’s emotional verdict)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final test of a novel is our affection for it—our human response—rather than purely abstract or academic measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentimentality is a danger (it should not speak too loudly or too soon), but the intensely human quality is essential; if humanity is exorcised, little remains but a bunch of words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspense as essential tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspense—the reader’s desire to know what will happen next—is the primal literary tool that secures attention and ties episodes together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suspense is ancient and fundamental; without it stories fail to hold popular audiences. Techniques like stopping mid-sentence (Scheherazade) are archetypal examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view and narrative technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Point of view and narrative manner (e.g., the use of 'he said'/'she said', first vs third person, conversational devices) are technical aspects that vary historically and greatly affect how characters and events read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques of conversation and attribution have changed over centuries and color the surroundings; choose technique fitting to tone and era you wish to evoke, and beware anachronistic attribution styles that jar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy (imaginative mode and method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy is a distinguishable aspect or mode of novel-writing exemplified by writers like Sterne and Virginia Woolf: starting from small objects or moments, fluttering off into associative, whimsical, or philosophically bewildered passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fantastical technique combines humorous appreciation of life’s muddle with keen sense of beauty; it relies on associative leaps, repetition of small obsessions, and deliberate bewilderment of direction—effective for particular temperaments but not universal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecy (novel’s insight into future or human change)
rubrics_metrics.description: The prophetic aspect concerns a novel’s capacity to apprehend or anticipate future mental states, social changes, or altered self-perception—an element of imaginative foresight or psychological discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forster treats prophecy as one aspect among seven: works with genuine prophetic power show sensory or psychological insight that may outlast their topical circumstances. (Section referenced in index: Prophecy defined, pp.125–126.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice and control of detail (visualisation and cataloguing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist’s selection and ordering of details (cataloguing visual particulars, domestic objects, social gestures) creates comic effects, social critique, and vivid scenes but can also expose poverty of taste if overdone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catalogues of detail are a powerful tool for social humor and visualization (Dickens/Wells examples). Use them to create effect but avoid excessive proximity of author to reader (which can feel low-quality or intrusive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-drawing methods ('novelist’s touch')
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is revealed by what the novelist chooses to show—the small incidents, habitual gestures, and the author's willingness to sit with the character—and by narrative tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should be read and presented through action and detail, not merely classed or paraphrased. The 'novelist’s touch'—subtle, precise phrasing and restraint—matters for convincing characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding pseudo-scholarship (critical method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism should not rely on superficial classification (chronology, locality, subject-matter categories) instead of close reading; pseudo-scholars classify books before they have read or understood them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: over-systematic classifications (novels by weather, by 'tone' with two categories, endless topical taxonomies). Good criticism reads books closely, resists trivial taxonomies, and cultivates a wide outlook to avoid provincialism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding provincialism (critic’s necessary wide outlook)
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic must avoid provincialism: criticism requires a wide outlook and knowledge of foreign achievement so as not to overvalue local or parochial works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forster warns critics against claiming English fiction as supreme; comparative perspective (Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, Proust) enriches judgment. Provincialism in a critic is a serious fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique change across generations (literary tradition matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques (humor, fantasy, conversation, use of 'he said'/'she said') change over generations; while the novelist’s psychological impulses may be stable, his techniques and traditions evolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-equipped critic will attend to literary tradition and technique shifts; practitioners should be aware that technique informs what readers perceive as similar or different across eras.
